#6150. We Tracked 133 Diverted Flights In Two Weeks: Here’s Where They Ended Up

Flight diversions are often treated as isolated incidents, but a closer look at two weeks of aviation activity reveals a much larger pattern. Between November 6 and 18, 133 flights diverted from their intended destinations, and several airports saw multiple waves of diversions within hours. Some aircraft landed relatively close to their original destinations, while others ended up thousands of kilometers away.

Simple Flying Flight Tracker data examined 63 diversion posts covering 133 flights, including 17 major diversion waves involving four or more aircraft from the same airport within an hour. From an 11-flight disruption at New York-JFK to a 13-aircraft scramble at San Francisco International Airport (SFO), the data reveals which airports absorbed the most diverted traffic, where airlines sent their aircraft, and which journeys experienced the most dramatic changes.

Thursday, November 12, was easily the busiest day in our tracking period, accounting for 35 of the 63 diversion posts. The disruptions were particularly concentrated around New York, where John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) saw an 11-flight diversion wave, along with numerous additional diversions involving transatlantic arrivals.

The disruption was noticeable among international operators. Aircraft arriving from Europe were redirected to airports across the northeastern United States, with Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) becoming the most frequently used alternative. Other aircraft were diverted to Bradley International Airport (BDL) in Connecticut, Philadelphia International Airport (PHL), Providence, and, of course, Bangor International Airport (BGR) in Maine, which has historically been a major diversion hotspot for many transatlantic flights. The diversions affected flights operated by several major airlines, including American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, British Airways, Air France, Lufthansa, and KLM Royal Dutch Airlines

The JFK disruption was not the only significant event that day. The neighboring Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) experienced a four-flight diversion wave, while PHL saw eight flights redirected. LaGuardia Airport (LGA) also recorded four diversions. Together, these events demonstrate how disruption at several airports in the same metropolitan region can create a complicated situation for airline operations. But with so many aircraft needing alternative landing locations, which airports handled the most diversions?

Boston was the most frequently used diversion airport during the tracking period, receiving 16 flights that had originally been scheduled to land elsewhere. Much of this traffic came from the November 12 disruption at JFK, when transatlantic arrivals were redirected to alternative airports across the northeastern United States.

Boston's geographical position made it a prominent destination in the diversion data. Several flights originally scheduled to land at JFK were redirected there, including services operated by American, Delta, British Airways, Air France, Emirates, and KLM. The affected routes included arrivals from London, Amsterdam, Paris Charles de Gaulle, Barcelona, Milan, and Dubai. However, Boston was not the only airport dealing with repeated waves of unexpected arrivals.

On the other side of the Atlantic, Katowice International Airport (KTW) in Poland came remarkably close to the top, receiving 15 diverted flights. The airport became an important alternative for aircraft originally scheduled to land at Krakow John Paul II International Airport (KRK), which experienced four separate diversion waves over four consecutive days. Back in the US, Fresno Yosemite International Airport (FAT) ranked third, receiving nine diverted aircraft, all tied to the major San Francisco disruption on November 18.

The geographical distribution is rather curious. Boston and Katowice were heavily affected by disruptions at nearby airports, while Fresno and Los Angeles benefited from their proximity to San Francisco. This raises another question: were these diversions isolated incidents, or were entire airports experiencing repeated operational disruptions?

From Gander to Shannon, these airports serve as aviation's ultimate safety nets, handling emergency diversions and ETOPS operations across the world

Krakow was one of the most interesting airports in the dataset, experiencing four separate diversion waves between November 6 and 9. Each wave involved at least four flights, with the aircraft redirected to several alternative airports across Poland and neighboring countries.

The first wave occurred late on November 6, when four aircraft originally scheduled to land at Krakow were redirected. Three ended up at Katowice, while the fourth landed at Rzeszow-Jasionka Airport (RZE). The following morning, another six flights were diverted, with five heading to Katowice and one returning to Frankfurt. This included aircraft operated by Ryanair, Wizz Air, and Finnair, demonstrating that the disruption affected multiple airlines and aircraft types.

The situation continued on November 8, when two further waves involved eight and five aircraft, respectively. Unlike the earlier events, these diversions were distributed across a wider selection of cities, including Warsaw, Wroclaw, Gdansk, Brno, and Ostrava. The final wave arrived on November 9, when another six flights were redirected, five of which landed at Katowice.

Katowice, Warsaw, Wroclaw, Gdansk, Rzeszow, Ostrava

Wroclaw, Warsaw-Modlin, Brno, Lodz, Ostrava

Katowice's 15-flight total is particularly revealing because it shows how an airport can become an important alternative landing point during repeated disruption at a nearby facility. However, Krakow was not the only airport to experience a concentrated wave of diversions. On November 18, events unfolded on the opposite side of the Atlantic, producing the largest individual diversion wave recorded in our dataset.

On November 18, SFO saw the largest individual diversion wave in our tracking period, with 13 flights redirected in about an hour. Nine aircraft landed at Fresno, while another four were sent to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

The scale of the event was striking because it involved both domestic and international services. Among the affected aircraft was Korean Air flight 23 from Seoul Incheon (ICN), which landed in LAX instead SFO. Other long-haul services included United Airlines flight 862 from Hong Kong, which also diverted to LAX, and United flight UA34 from Osaka Kansai, which followed the same route.

Domestic arrivals were affected too. JetBlue flight 633 from BOS and AA76 from JFK both landed at Fresno. DL668, arriving from JFK, was among the aircraft redirected to LAX. The nine-flight Fresno total made it the most frequently used alternative airport during the San Francisco event.

The November 18 San Francisco diversion wave:

Fresno Yosemite International Airport (FAT)

Fresno's role and location are noteworthy. Although it is considerably smaller than San Francisco and Los Angeles, it absorbed most of the diverted aircraft in this event. This shows how diversion planning can extend beyond a region's largest airports, depending on operational circumstances and available alternatives. However, the San Francisco wave was not the only event involving unusually long journeys to alternative airports. Some aircraft in our dataset ended up nowhere near their original destinations.

Though necessary, they can be frustrating for passengers and crew.

Although many diversions involved relatively short journeys to nearby airports, several flights in our dataset experienced substantially longer route changes. The most dramatic example involved KL677, which was operating from AMS to Calgary International Airport (YYC).

On November 9, the Boeing 787 operating the service landed at Keflavik International Airport (KEF), in Iceland, approximately 3,200 miles (5,132 kilometers) short of its intended destination. This was the longest diversion recorded in our dataset. The distance illustrates just how significant the operational consequences of a diversion can become when an aircraft is already deep into a long-haul journey.

United Airlines flight UA114 experienced the second-longest diversion. The service was scheduled to fly from Papeete International Airport (PPT), in French Polynesia, to San Francisco, but instead landed at Honolulu International Airport (HNL). The aircraft arrived about (2,400 miles) 3,857 kilometers short of San Francisco, leaving passengers in Hawaii instead of the intended Californian destination.

The third-largest diversion involved easyJet flight 7883, operating from AMS to Tenerife South Airport (TFS). Instead of reaching the Canary Islands, the aircraft landed at Paris Orly Airport (ORY), approximately 1,750 miles (2,814 kilometers) from its intended destination, much closer to the departure airport. The flight was unusual because it involved a European short-haul operator and a diversion just within 300 miles (about 500 km) of the departure point.

These examples demonstrate that a diversion does not necessarily mean landing at the nearest available airport. Long-haul operations can involve complex considerations, and aircraft operating across different regions may have to use alternative airports far from their original destinations. But how representative are these individual examples of the overall diversion picture?

The 133 flights recorded between November 6 and 18 provide an interesting snapshot of how quickly disruption can spread across airline networks. Simple Flying's tracking identified 63 separate diversion posts, including 17 major waves in which at least four aircraft were diverted from the same airport within an hour. The dataset also contained 45 long-haul diversion posts and one short-haul diversion involving easyJet.

It is important to distinguish between the number of posts and the number of flights. A single diversion-wave post could cover several aircraft, while individual long-haul diversions were also reported separately. Some long-haul flights were included in the larger waves, meaning the figures should not be added together as independent flight totals. ADS-B tracking independently confirmed the landing airports for every flight included in the spreadsheet.

Simple Flying Flight Tracker's social channels regularly publish individual diversions and larger waves of disrupted flights as they happen. They offer a useful way to follow unexpected changes to airline operations in real time.

The most interesting finding isn't that 133 aircraft landed somewhere other than their planned destinations. It is how concentrated some of the disruption became. Boston absorbed 16 diverted flights, Katowice received 15, and Fresno handled nine aircraft during a single event at San Francisco. With individual waves involving as many as 13 aircraft, the data reminds us that an airport's operational importance can change dramatically when another facility is disrupted.

#6149. Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

#6148. Why JSX Just Bought New Pacific Airlines, The Strange, Failed 757 Startup

Public charter air carrier JSX has just acquired New Pacific Airlines, and with this, New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights, with Embraer E145 aircraft.

If you’re not familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “huh?” If you are familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “WTF?” There’s a sneaky and logical explanation here, so let me explain.

Let’s start with a little context. JSX is a public charter air carrier, which operates a fleet of nearly 60 planes, most of which are Embraer E135s and E145s.

It operates as a Part 135 operator, meaning it’s not technically an airline, as it’s using a loophole that allows it to not use standard TSA security screening, hire pilots with fewer than 1,500 hours, etc. Basically what’s happening is that one subsidiary sells the tickets, and then another subsidiary operates the flights, so it’s technically a “charter” (with 30 people who don’t know one another).

Then there’s New Pacific Airlines, one of the strangest airline startups we’ve ever seen, and which I’ve covered extensively. The airline acquired some Boeing 757s, and the business plan was to connect North America and Asia via Anchorage (ANC).

The business model made zero sense in the first place, though there was some funding there, and they even invested in constructing a lounge in Anchorage, even though those flights never did happen. The airline did briefly fly from (ONT) to Nashville (BNA) — as one does — before ultimately going out of business.

That brings us to the news. New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with Embraer E145s that are leased from JSX, as reported by IshrionA. According to a Department of Transportation filing, the airline intends to resume flights with planes featuring 42 seats, which is higher than the 30-seat limit you’ll find on current JSX planes.

JSX acquires New Pacific Airlines.New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with ERJ 145 leased from JSX. pic.twitter.com/uMMS0J2fZy

On the surface, this of course makes absolutely no sense. New Pacific Airlines was out of business, and the business model made no sense. So why would JSX buy an airline and then lease planes to it?

Long story short, this seems to be a play to acquire a cheap Part 121 certificate. A Part 121 operator is a company that’s allowed to operate scheduled air transport… in other words, a “real” airline. As I mentioned above, JSX has historically been a Part 135 operator, and that explicitly means it’s not an airline. It’s a public charter air carrier, so it’s not a “real” airline.

Going back a couple of years, we know that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) was considering cracking down on carriers like JSX, since they definitely don’t operate within the spirit of the rules. That’s not to say that JSX did anything wrong, because by the letter of the law, they’re following it exactly. It’s just that the letter of the law makes no sense, and clearly doesn’t reflect the intent behind distinguishing between Part 121 and Part 135 operators.

Under Trump, there was no scrutiny of this. However, with Democrats soon controlling both the House and Senate, I imagine JSX leaders may be worried that there could again be more scrutiny. If nothing else, buying a cheap Part 121 certificate is a good insurance policy, in case the government does crack down. After all, these can basically be “sold,” while acquiring one from scratch can be grueling process.

I wouldn’t assume that anything will really operate with New Pacific Airlines branding, or based on a New Pacific Airlines business model. Instead, I imagine the idea is that JSX will start dabbling in Part 121 operations, which is why these planes will have more seats (above the 30-seat cap that’s allowed), since that’s no longer a factor.

If the government were to crack down on Part 135 operators, JSX could move to Part 121 operations. However, they’d have to make lots of changes, from their pilot hiring, to the way passengers are screened.

JSX has just bought New Pacific, the airline with an absurd business model that went bankrupt. No, JSX isn’t inspired by the concept of flying Boeing 757s to Asia. Instead, this is clearly the cheapest way for JSX to acquire a Part 121 certificate, which would be required for the carrier to continue operations in the event that the government were to crack down on the Part 135 operator loophole.

It’s going to be interesting to see how this evolves, both since JSX seems to have plans to operate Part 121 operations in the near future, and also to see how JSX’s business model would evolve if the Part 135 concept were blocked.

What do you make of this JSX Part 121 play?

Taking a cruise is even better when you get a great deal — and if you’re looking to book right now for a cruise (or cruises) in 2027 and beyond, your timing couldn’t be better. Cruise lines have launched Black Friday deals that include discounted fares, cabin upgrades, third- and fourth-guest-free promos, and onboard credits.

We’ve found the best promotions from leading ocean and river cruise lines, lesser-known small-ship operators and expedition brands. So whether your goal is beach time in the Caribbean, wildlife-spotting in Alaska, seeing the northern lights in the Arctic or enjoying culture and cuisine along Europe’s rivers, there’s a deal for every type of cruiser.

When considering Black Friday offers, however, remember that cruise demand remains high, so selection may be limited and fares — especially on the newest ships — will likely be pricier than in years past. To truly get a good deal, make sure you’re comfortable with the final price quoted, including the exact fare per person and the value of any added perks, before booking. Calling the cruise line’s reservations department may help clarify any questions.

Here’s a look at the Black Friday deals being offered by more than 40 cruise lines. Check back soon for Cyber Monday deal updates.

Through Dec. 3, AmaWaterways has a Black Friday offer that lets you choose between a complimentary pre- or postcruise land package or cruise fare savings of up to $2,500 per cabin (double occupancy). You’ll also receive a free cabin upgrade on select 2027 and 2028 sailings in Europe and South America.

Small-ship operator American Cruise Lines’ current cruise deals and special offers include free domestic airfare and savings of $1,000 to $2,000 per cabin on select late 2026 and 2027 departures. This applies to its eight-night Florida Gulf Coast and Keys sailings, eight-night Southeast Sea Islands cruises, eight-night Columbia and Snake River sailings, and eight-night Lower Mississippi River cruises.

From Nov. 24 to 28, you can enjoy Black Friday savings of up to 55% on select expedition cruises from Atlas Ocean Voyages and also receive air credit savings of up to $2,000 per suite on qualifying voyages. Through Nov. 23, guests and travel advisers may also submit priority reservations for eligible expeditions on the Atlas Ocean Voyages website ahead of the five-day Black Friday promotional event. Reservations will begin confirming Nov. 24, subject to availability, with Atlas Yacht Club members receiving first priority to secure special Black Friday savings once the sale begins.

Through Dec. 12, Avalon Waterways is offering a Black Friday Sales Event featuring free gratuities and free airfare on select 2027 European river cruises. Avalon’s offer also includes savings of up to $2,000 per couple on a Panorama or Royal Suite upgrade on certain 2027 departures.

The Black Friday Flash Sale at Azamara, available now through Dec. 4, includes up to $6,000 off per cabin on select sailings in the Mediterranean, South America, Japan and Alaska, plus up to $750 in onboard credit per cabin. The deal is valid on all four Azamara ships for sailings from January 2027 to April 2028. You can book a sale voyage online or via a travel adviser.

Carnival's Black Friday deals span Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday with promotions that include discounted fares (four-night sailings start at under $200 per person), $49 per person deposits, room upgrades starting at $1, "Kids Sail Free" offers on select cruises (in third and fourth bunks), discounted beverage and Wi-Fi and shore excursion packages, and up to $50 in onboard credits. Sales and promotions are rolling out through Dec. 1.

Celebrity Cruises has a rolling Black Friday promotion offering savings of 75% on the second guest in the cabin on hundreds of applicable sailings in 2027 and 2028, including Caribbean and Mediterranean voyages on its newest ship, Celebrity Xcel. There are also limited-time offers that include up to $1,000 in additional savings per cabin plus $100 savings on select European sailings. This offer, for example, is valid through Nov. 24.

Through Dec. 2, Greek cruise line Celestyal has a “Big Sailaway” Black Friday promotion offering savings of up to 50%, plus third and fourth guests in a cabin sail free, on 58 Mediterranean and Greek islands voyages (from three nights to 14 nights) departing between March 2027 and February 2028. Celestyal operates two mid-size ships, Celestyal Journey and Celestyal Discovery.

Italy-based Costa Cruises is celebrating the start of the holiday season with a Black Friday sale offering fares as low as $399 per person (double occupancy) on select departures through June 2027, when reserved by Nov. 30. The included regions are the Caribbean (on Costa Fascinosa and Costa Favolosa), the Canary Islands (on Costa Smeralda) and the Mediterranean (on Costa Pacifica, Costa Toscana, Costa Smeralda, Costa Fascinosa and Costa Favolosa).

Through Dec. 7, small luxury cruise line Cruise Croatia is offering Black Friday savings of up to $500 per cabin on select seven-night spring and summer 2027 Adriatic sailings between Dubrovnik and Split, Croatia.

Book by Dec. 2 to take advantage of the Seasonal Savings deal offered by luxury cruise line Crystal. It can save you up to 40% on more than 200 upcoming voyages worldwide on Crystal Serenity or Crystal Symphony. The discount applies only to the first and second guest in a cabin. Full World Cruise and Full Grand Journeys are excluded.

Through Dec. 7, the Cunard Black Friday event can save you up to 40% on select sailings aboard Cunard's four ships — Queen Elizabeth, Queen Victoria, Queen Mary 2 and Queen Anne — with fares starting at $999 per person. Plus, you’ll enjoy a 10% refundable deposit and an onboard credit. Deals are available on Caribbean, Northern Europe, Mediterranean, transatlantic and Canada sailings. Guests booking Grill Suites will also have their Hotel Charge waived.

Although Disney Cruise Line doesn’t have Black Friday-specific deals, it is currently offering savings of up to 25% on select Caribbean sailings from Fort Lauderdale, Port Canaveral and Galveston, Texas; it's also offering deals on Mexican Riviera sailings from San Diego. These three- to seven-night cruises must be booked under the "guaranteed stateroom with restrictions" category. (In this case, "guaranteed" means you can’t select your specific room, but you're guaranteed one in the category you’ve booked or higher.) Your specific cabin will be assigned at a later date, but a full, nonrefundable payment is due at the time of booking.

Through Dec. 1, save up to 40% with Black Friday offers when you book select sailings with luxury cruise line Explora Journeys. Choose from two options: Full Payment Fare with savings of up to 40% (full payment is required at the time of reservation and is nonrefundable and cannot be changed), or Flexible Fare with savings of up to 30% (a 5% deposit is required, and standard cancellation policies apply).

Grand Circle Cruise Line is offering Black Friday sales to travelers 50 and older with savings of up to $3,000 per person on select January to July 2027 river cruises in Europe. Or you can get a $500 per-person discount plus an additional 10% off all 2027 departures when you pay in full. You can reserve by Nov. 30 by calling 800-221-2610 with code "BLACKFRIDAY26."

Available through Nov. 29, the Black Friday offer from Holland America Line is valid on more than 800 cruises to destinations worldwide, departing from December 2026 through spring 2029. The promotion includes up to 30% off cruise fares, free prepaid crew appreciation, 50% reduced deposits and free or reduced third and fourth guests in the same cabin. You can also combine the Black Friday offer with Holland America’s "Have it All" premium fare, which adds four high-value amenities: shore excursions, specialty dining, Wi-Fi and a beverage package.

Available through Dec. 2, Hurtigruten’s annual Black Friday sale offers savings of up to 50% on its 2027 Original Voyages, including the Coastal Express, which has cruised the Norwegian coast since 1893. Hurtigruten is also offering savings of up to 30% on its all-inclusive Signature Voyages in 2027, which include the North Cape Line and the Svalbard Line.

Through Dec. 2, HX Expeditions (formerly Hurtigruten Expeditions) is offering as much as 40% off select departures from late 2026 to 2028 with its Black Friday promotion. The sale offers savings on more than 50 all-inclusive expedition cruises to some of the world’s most remote destinations, including Antarctica, Greenland, Svalbard, the Galapagos Islands and the Northwest Passage.

Through Nov. 29, you can enjoy 60% off thanks to Black Friday savings on eligible itineraries through 2028 across the Jimmy Buffett-inspired Margaritaville at Sea fleet, plus third and fourth guests cruise for free on select sailings. These deals include sailings on the new Margaritaville at Sea Beachcomber, debuting in January 2027, as well as a buy-one-get-one deal on $499 Cruise Certificates that you can use on future voyages.

Through Nov. 30, receive a free veranda upgrade, plus a $250 onboard credit per cabin on eight Mitsui Ocean Cruises voyages sailing from February to April 2027. Mitsui operates two 458-guest, all-suite ships (formerly part of the Seabourn fleet) that are centered on authentic Japanese hospitality. It offers six- to 12-night itineraries in Japan that call on ports rarely visited by larger cruise lines. Both Japanese and English are spoken on board.

MSC Cruises' Black Friday sale is available through Nov. 27 and includes up to 40% off most 2027 itineraries around the world, plus up to $1,000 onboard credit, a free balcony upgrade and a "kids sail free" offer.

The Black Friday sale at Norwegian Cruise Line offers 50% off all cruises, plus a Free at Sea™ package. The offer is valid through Dec. 1 and applies to all itineraries, which visit nearly 350 destinations. The offer is good for all ships, including the cruise line’s two newest vessels: Norwegian Luna, which debuted in 2026, and Norwegian Aura, set to launch in spring 2027. Norwegian’s Free at Sea™ package on a standard seven-night sailing offers amenities that total more than $2,000 in savings. Such amenities include unlimited open bar access with premium spirits, unlimited Wi-Fi, three multicourse specialty dining meals for the first and second guest on the reservation, and $50 off each shore excursion for the first guest on the reservation.

Book by Dec. 1 to enjoy up to 50% savings on more than 200 Oceania Cruises voyages in 2027, thanks to the line’s Black Friday sale. The deal is available across the Oceania fleet, including its three newest ships: Oceania Vista (launched in 2023), Oceania Allura (launched in 2025) and Oceania Sonata (debuting in August 2027). Also included is Oceania Aurelia, the former Oceania Nautica, which is being refurbished and renamed ahead of its relaunch in late 2027.

Book during the Black Friday Savings event through Nov. 30 to save $1,500 to $10,000 per person on select 2027 Overseas Adventure Travel small ship ocean cruises. All 2027 departures are also eligible for savings of $500 per person plus an additional 10% when you pay in full. Discounted itineraries include small-ship adventures to Antarctica, the Baltic, the Adriatic, the Mediterranean, Egypt and the British Isles. Call 800-955-1925 and use code "BLACKFRIDAY26" to book.

The holiday sale from Tahiti-based Paul Gauguin Cruises offers savings of 10% on all 2027 departures to Polynesian destinations like the Society Islands, Tuamotus, Cook Islands and Marquesas. Cruises must be booked by Jan. 4, 2027.

Expedition cruise line Ponant Explorations has a holiday sale offering savings of up to 20% on most 2027 voyages in alliance with Smithsonian Journeys — the travel program of the Smithsonian Institution designed for immersive exploration and educational enrichment. Book through Jan. 4 using code "HOLIDAYSJ." The holiday sale also offers 10% savings on a wide selection of Ponant Explorations sailings to destinations such as the Panama Canal, Costa Rica and Madagascar. Use the code "HOLIDAY26" when booking.

Princess' “Blue Friday” sale runs through Dec. 7 and features up to 50% off cruise fares on select voyages to destinations such as the Caribbean, Alaska, Mexico, the Mediterranean and Asia. This includes itineraries on the cruise line’s two newest ships, Sun Princess and Star Princess. Additionally, third and fourth guests in a cabin sail free, and cruisers can enjoy up to $400 in instant savings.

From now until Dec. 3, save up to 40% on select Quark Expeditions voyages to the Arctic and Antarctica during its Black Friday sale. Limited cabins are available for Antarctic 2026-27 and Arctic 2027 expeditions, so check the deals if you’re looking to enjoy a polar expedition cruise to Patagonia and the Antarctic Peninsula or Greenland and Svalbard, Norway.

Luxury small-ship cruise line Regent Seven Seas Cruises is offering "The Black Friday Collection" — a limited-time offer of up to 40% savings on more than 60 voyages worldwide, including sailings in Europe, Alaska and Asia, if booked by Dec. 1. The promotion also includes $500 onboard credit per suite.

From Nov. 23 to Dec. 4, European river cruise line Riverside Luxury Cruises is offering 10% off full-board fares on select 2027 and 2028 sailings of five nights or longer during its Black Friday sale. You can combine this promotion with existing offers (Early Booking, Long Stay and Repeat Guest) for combined savings of up to 43%. All discounts will be applied at the time of booking; no code needed.

Through Dec. 7, U.K.-based Riviera Travel River Cruises is offering North American travelers a Black Friday sale with up to 50% off all 2027 and 2028 sailings and half-price deposits. For example, seven-night river cruises start at $1,999 per person (reduced from about $3,000 per person). Riviera will introduce two new ships in September 2027: MS Riviera Reflection on the Danube River and MS Riviera Alba on the Mekong River. It will also debut the world’s first solo-traveler-dedicated river ship, MS George Eliot, in June 2027. All Riviera ships qualify for Black Friday discounts.

Through Dec. 7, Royal Caribbean is offering Black Friday promotions and flash deals, including instant savings of up to $1,000 on select cruise fares, plus third and fourth guests in a cabin can sail free. These deals also include onboard credit starting at $150 and up to 50% savings on beverage packages, Wi-Fi and shore excursions. Savings, which vary by cabin and itinerary length, are available on more than 25 Royal Caribbean ships, including the line’s newest megaships — Legend of the Seas, Star of the Seas, Icon of the Seas and Utopia of the Seas. These ships sail to destinations in the Caribbean, Alaska and Europe.

Book by Nov. 29 to score Black Friday savings of up to 40% off cruise fares on select 2027 and 2028 river and ocean itineraries offered by Scenic Luxury Cruises and Tours. Scenic operates river ships and luxury expedition ocean vessels. Sale destinations include Europe’s top rivers, the Mediterranean and the Caribbean. To book, call Scenic’s reservations team at 844-323-1917.

Bookable through Dec. 8, the Black Friday deals from Seabourn Cruise Line are available for nearly all sailings through 2029 on Seabourn’s five luxury ships; offers include a free two-category Veranda Suite upgrade, plus up to a $2,000 shipboard credit per suite (for Penthouse Suites and above) and up to $500 shipboard credit per suite (for Oceanview and Veranda suites). The deal also includes a 15% reduced deposit on nearly all voyages.

Through Dec. 1, SeaDream Yacht Club, which operates two 112-guest yachts in the Caribbean, Mediterranean and Northern Europe, has a "Sail Away" promotion offering up to 25% off on select 2027 voyages. Use the code "SAILAWAY26" when booking.

With the Black Friday sale from luxury ocean and expedition line Silversea Cruises, you can save up to 45% on more than 850 sailings through May 2029 if you book by Dec. 7. By reserving now, you can also secure your suite with reduced deposits that start at 15%.

If you book a qualifying Star Clippers 2027 or 2028 Mediterranean voyage that visits Sicily by Dec. 31, the cruise line will offer a $500 (or $600 Canadian dollars) air credit and a complimentary 3GB Wi-Fi package per cabin. The offer is valid for North American residents booking a Category 2 to 6 cabin on one of Star Clippers' three sailing vessels: the 227-guest Royal Clipper, the 166-guest Star Clipper or the 166-guest Star Flyer. For qualifying sailings, reservations and questions, contact a travel adviser, call Star Clippers at 800-442-0551 or visit the Star Clippers website.

Through Dec. 4, expedition cruise line Swan Hellenic is offering up to $4,000 per person in Black Friday savings on 24 voyages worldwide, plus an additional $250 per person onboard credit. The eligible voyages sail to some of the world’s most remote places — including destinations in Antarctica, Africa, Asia Pacific and the Arctic — from March 9 to Oct. 27, 2027. Returning guests receive 10% loyalty savings, and back-to-back bookings earn a 5% discount.

Trafalgar has Black Friday deals, including BOGO 50%-off fares on featured European river sailings. The eligible 2027 itineraries, available through Dec. 3, change weekly (every Thursday), while other select departures are available at a 20% discount. Call 866-513-1995 to book, and make sure to mention Black Friday BOGO.

Luxury all-inclusive river cruise line Uniworld Boutique River Cruises — which offers sailings in Europe, Egypt, South America and Asia — has a Black Friday offer bookable through Dec. 18: The second guest pays 50% of the cruise fare when booking at double occupancy. This “Journey Together” offer is valid for select sailings throughout 2027 and is combinable with River Heritage Club member benefits for previous guests.

Family-owned, small-ship cruise line Variety Cruises has a Black Friday sale offering travelers up to 50% off on new reservations made through Dec. 7. Deals are available for seven-, 10- and 11-night cruises on Variety’s recently refurbished fleet of small ships (which hold no more than 49 guests). Available itineraries range from the Seychelles and Tahiti to signature Mediterranean voyages in Greece, Italy, Malta and destinations along the Adriatic coast.

Book any 2027 Victory Cruise Lines voyage by Nov. 30 to save $500 per person. Victory offers all-inclusive, small-ship cruises on the Great Lakes, coastal Canada, the U.S. East Coast and Florida.

While not technically a Black Friday promotion, Viking is offering its "lowest fares of the season" on select 2027 and 2028 river, ocean and expedition itineraries. River fares start at $1,999 per person, with reduced airfares and $25 deposits (just be sure to book by Nov. 27 with offer code "PLR27"). Ocean sailings are up to 35% off, with reduced airfare and $25 deposits (book by Nov. 30). Expedition voyages are up to 15% off, with reduced airfare and $25 deposits (book by Nov. 30).

Through Dec. 3, Virgin Voyages has a “buy one, get the second at 80% off” cruise fare promotion. Plus, you can score up to a $600 bar tab (depending on the length of the voyage) to cover onboard beverages. The deal is available for all cruises on Virgin’s four ships, including its first-ever Baltic sailings from Amsterdam on Valiant Lady in summer 2028. The promotion automatically applies when booking via the Virgin Voyages website.

Bookable through Dec. 2, the "Thankful for Travel Sales Event" offered by Windstar Cruises includes a complimentary all-inclusive package (which includes wine, beer, cocktails, Wi-Fi and gratuities, and is worth up to $1,386 per couple on a seven-night cruise). This applies to select sailings in the Mediterranean, Caribbean, Tahiti and Latin America through March 31, 2027. The promotion also lets you reserve with a $300 reduced deposit and gives you a $300 onboard credit.

In addition to booking directly with a cruise line, you can also reach out to a travel adviser to secure your reservation. Advisers have access to the same great deals that the lines are offering, but sometimes they can throw in extras, such as free bottles of wine or onboard credits. Before booking anything directly, it might be worth a phone call.

#6146. Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

#6145. Buy Southwest Rapid Rewards Points For 50% Off (1.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

Looking to buy Southwest points? Rapid Rewards is currently offering up to a 50% discount on purchased points, which is an opportunity to acquire them for just 1.5 cents each. Is that a good deal?

While there has long been value in strategically buying points, the concept of a revenue based frequent flyer program selling points can be tougher to rationalize. So that I don’t bury the lede, let me say that I’d only buy points in a very narrow set of circumstances, like if trying to top off a points balance for a specific redemption.

Link: Buy Southwest Rapid Rewards points with this promotion for 50% off

Between 12:01AM CT on November 19 and 11:59PM CT on December 31, 2026, Southwest Rapid Rewards is offering a discount on purchased points. With Southwest, it’s common for different members to be eligible for different offers, so you’ll have to log into your Rapid Rewards account to see what you’re eligible for.

However, the best version of the offer to buy Southwest points provides up to a 50% discount, structured as follows:

Ordinarily you can buy Southwest points for 3.0 cents each, and that price is inclusive of the 7.5% federal excise tax. Given the limit of being able to purchase up to 100,000 Rapid Rewards points per day, that means if you maxed out this promotion, you could buy 100,000 points for $1,500, which is a cost of 1.5 cents per point.

Southwest sells points in increments of 1,000 points, with 2,000 points being the minimum. Ordinarily there’s a daily maximum of buying 60,000 points, but during this promotion, that cap has been increased to 100,000 points.

Just in the interest of being thorough, some Rapid Rewards members may be eligible for smaller percentage discounts, so let me crunch the numbers on those potential offers:

Southwest has no annual limit on how many Rapid Rewards points you can buy. The only restriction is that you can ordinarily buy at most 60,000 points per calendar day. During this promotion, that cap has been increased to 100,000 points, though.

Note that the purchase of Southwest points is non-refundable, and buying Southwest points doesn’t count toward Rapid Rewards elite status or Companion Pass qualification. Purchased points typically post nearly instantly, but in some cases, it can take up to 72 hours for them to post.

Southwest Rapid Rewards frequently offers promotions on purchasing points. When the program does have a buy points promotion, the 50% discount offer is pretty standard. So I’d recommend buying points based on when you have a relatively immediate use for redeeming them, rather than anything else.

Below is a chart with some of the recent Southwest buy points promotions that we’ve seen, before this one.

If you’d like to buy Southwest Airlines points, note that purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore this wouldn’t be treated as a Southwest purchase if you’re using a Rapid Rewards credit card.

I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue based frequent flyer program, and the number of points required for a flight is roughly correlated to the revenue cost of a flight. However, there is a dynamic element to the pricing, whereby the value you get per point varies significantly, based on the flight and fare class you redeem for. With this, we’re seeing redemption values as low as 1.1 cents per point, and as high as 1.5 cents per point, give or take.

As you can tell, there are probably few situations where it makes sense to buy points for 1.5 cents (or more) each, when they can’t be redeemed for that, best case scenario.

Let me cut to the chase — there are few situations where it makes sense to purchase Rapid Rewards points. Even at the discounted cost, there’s not usually value in buying points for 1.5 cents each when you can typically only redeem them for less than that. So don’t buy these points speculatively, unless you know exactly what you’re doing, and have a redemption in mind.

There are three potential scenarios I’d like to address, including the main scenario where I think it could make sense (but not really), which is to build up a balance of Southwest points, given the flexibility this provides.

Some might buy Rapid Rewards points in order to top off their account so they have enough points for a Rapid Rewards award ticket. I guess this might be worth it to some if you need a small number of points, though personally I’d just keep collecting points and then redeem with your next ticket.

The Southwest Airlines Companion Pass is one of the best values in domestic travel. If you qualify for this, you can always have a companion travel with you for just the standard taxes, regardless of whether you’re booking a cash ticket or redeeming points.

For those with a Companion Pass, buying Southwest points could get you outsized value:

However, there’s still absolutely zero reason to do that. You’d be better off just booking a paid ticket and then having a companion fly with you.

There is one major benefit in general to paying for a ticket with Southwest Rapid Rewards points rather than cash. While Southwest Airlines has no change fees on both revenue and award tickets on most kinds of fares:

I do think there’s big value in having a stash of Rapid Rewards points. I use this when I speculatively want to book travel (including for friends and family), since there’s no downside.

If you’re looking to earn Southwest points, there are plenty of ways to rack up this currency with credit card rewards:

On top of that, Rapid Rewards has a variety of co-branded Chase credit cards, which can be a great way to rack up rewards. This includes cards like the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (learn more), Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more), etc.

Through December 31, 2026, Southwest is selling Rapid Rewards points with a discount of up to 50%, which brings the cost down to as little as 1.5 cents per point. I still don’t think there are many circumstances under which it makes sense to buy points, given that Rapid Rewards is a revenue based frequent flyer program, and points can typically only be redeemed for 1.1-1.5 cents each toward the cost of a ticket.

Under what circumstances do you think it’s worth buying Southwest Airlines points?

#6144. All The Destinations Delta Air Lines Is Flying Its Rare Boeing 767-400ERs To In 2026

Currently, only United Airlines and Delta Air Lines operate the Boeing 767-400ER as a scheduled passenger aircraft, although a VIP-configured airframe also operates for the Bahrain Royal Flight (Bahrain Air Force). While the -400ER is now a previous-generation aircraft with relatively high fuel consumption, it remains competitive within the Delta and United ecosystems for several reasons.

These include being paid off (low capital and lease expenses); lower maintenance, tooling, and training expenses due to commonality with broader 757 and 767 fleets; and being able to fill very specific niches that no other aircraft on the market offers. Its closest modern equivalents are the 787-8 Dreamliner, the Airbus A330-800neo, and A330-900neo. That said, the A330-800neo almost doesn't count, as it's so unpopular that almost no airline is seriously considering it anymore. Here is what to know about where Delta is flying its 767-400ERs, according to data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

Delta is one of the world's largest airlines by several measures, with a mainline fleet of 1,009 aircraft, according to Planespotters.net. It is also one of the primary remaining operators of the now-aging 767 family of passenger aircraft, with 57 examples in inventory. This is made up of 36 767-300ERs, whose average fleet age is now 29.7 years, and 21 767-400ERs with an average age of 26 years.

These were orders Delta placed itself. Delta inherited many aircraft from Northwest, but Northwest passed on the 767, citing its DC-10 fleet and cargo container compatibility—and instead chose A330-200s and A330-300s alongside its 747s and 757s. The 767-400ER was one of the least successful airliner variants Boeing has developed in modern times.

Boeing sold 1,451 examples of its 767 family, of which only 59 were the 767-400ER. It is unclear if Boeing ever recovered its expenses and broke even on the cost of developing the stretch. Regardless, the variant is now operated almost exclusively by Delta and United, for whom the aircraft fills a particular niche, making it difficult to replace. Both airlines apparently plan to operate the type for as long as is feasible.

According to Cirium data, Delta is operating 12,308 flights with its fleet of 767-400ERs this year, including return flights. They carry a total of 2.9 million seats and generate about 11 billion available seat miles (ASMs). The average route distance is 3,245 nautical miles.

The vast majority of these flights are operated from two Delta hubs: Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) and John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). ATL has 2,934 outbound flights and 700,000 outbound seats, and JFK has 3,183 outbound flights and 758,000 outbound seats. There are some limited short-haul routes under 500 nautical miles from Atlanta, but not from JFK.

Delta 767-400ER: Top 8 Routes By Frequency

The 767-400ER's regular routes are within the 2,000 to 4,300 nautical mile range, with the aircraft sometimes used to plug gaps on short routes or to run short routes between its longer-haul schedules. Overall, it is useful to think of the aircraft as a transatlantic workhorse as well as a lesser transcontinental workhorse. Only three pairings have more than 1,000 annual flights, and only one has more than 500 flights.

Delta deploys its 767s primarily on long-haul transcontinental and transatlantic routes.

All of Delta's shortest 767-400ER routes under 1,000 nautical miles are from its Atlanta hub, ignoring the ATL-JFK pairing. The shortest route is Atlanta to Orlando at just 350 nautical miles, with a total of 62 flights in both directions (outbound and inbound) for the year. Just three nautical miles longer is the Atlanta to Tampa pairing, with 20 flights covering 353 nautical miles.

Delta conducted eight flights between Atlanta and Detroit (516 nautical miles) and about 206 flights between Atlanta and Miami (517 nautical miles), meaning Florida dominates the shortest-route destinations. After Miami, the next shortest route is ATL to JFK, with 175 flights at 660 nautical miles. The only other destinations under 1,000 nautical miles are from Atlanta to Minneapolis-St. Paul at 787 nautical miles, although this route only sees four flights.

In the 1,000-1,999 nautical mile category, from and to Atlanta, there are 136 flights with Phoenix (1,379 nautical miles), 20 flights with Las Vegas (1,518 nautical miles), four flights with San Diego (1,643 nautical miles), 145 flights with Los Angeles (1,691 nautical miles), and 12 flights with San Francisco (1,859 nautical miles). Besides Atlanta, there are two flights between New York-JFK and Phoenix (1,871 nautical miles) and a single flight from Las Vegas to New York (1,953 nautical miles).

Moving above 2,000 nautical miles is the first very busy route, the transcontinental route between New York-JFK and Los Angeles with 1,617 flights at 2,151 nautical miles. JFK's 2,247-nautical-mile route to San Francisco sees 96 flights. The 767-400ER is one of the workhorses for Delta's transatlantic routes. It has the range to connect the East Coast with many of Western Europe's top destinations.

Next, transatlantic routes start from JFK. There are 173 flights (including return) to Dublin (2,763 nautical miles), 80 to Edinburgh (2,829 nautical miles), 137 to Lisbon (2,926 nautical miles), and 423 to London Heathrow (3,000 nautical miles). Going over 3,000 nautical miles, JFK's transatlantic pairings include Madrid (436 flights), Paris (1,117 flights), Barcelona (200 flights), and Zurich (483 flights).

These destinations are between 3,120 and 3,416 nautical miles. Finally, Atlanta sees its first transatlantic route to Dublin with 78 total flights. The other flight pairings under 3,500 nautical miles include New York and Nice (430 flights), New York and Milan Malpensa (387 flights), and a single flight from Atlanta to Edinburgh. ​​​​​​​

The airline will redeploy a significant portion of its 767-400ER fleet from domestic routes to services to and from Europe, affecting several routes.

Moving above 3,500 nautical miles, the first and only major route not to include New York or Atlanta is the 3,611-nautical-mile pairing between Cincinnati and Paris (250 flights). This is the same distance as Delta's New York to Venice pairing (451 flights). The next ten routes by distance (3,767 nautical miles to 4,132 nautical miles) are all from Delta's Atlanta hub.

In order of distance, these are London Heathrow (1,527 flights), Madrid (288 flights), Marrakech (127 flights), Paris (426 flights), Brussels (187 flights), and Barcelona (198 flights). After Barcelona, the routes are greater than 4,000 nautical miles and include Zurich (292 flights), Rio de Janeiro (315 flights), Nice (306 flights), and Milan (387 flights).

The Atlanta-Rio de Janeiro pairing is the first non-European international destination by ascending distance. Delta also operates 18 flights on its New York-Rio de Janeiro pairing, which is only marginally longer than the Atlanta pairing. Next, there are 652 flights between Atlanta and Munich and 197 flights between Atlanta and Venice.

The top five longest Delta 767-400ER routes are all over 4,250 nautical miles, but the frequencies are low. The New York-Athens pairing sees 135 flights over 4,294 nautical miles. Next is Atlanta to Buenos Aires with 95 flights. Delta typically assigns A330s and A350-900s on its Atlanta to Buenos Aires route. After Atlanta to Buenos Aires, there are no more regular flights.

There are two flights between Las Vegas and London Heathrow, two flights between New York and Buenos Aires, and a single flight from Paris to Las Vegas. The latter is the longest flight at 4,730 nautical miles. Delta's A330-900neos are the primary aircraft serving the Buenos Aires-New York route. It seems that with these routes (as well as very short routes), the 767-400ER is occasionally used to fill in when the aircraft typically assigned to the route are lacking.

According to Boeing, the 767-400ER has a basic range of 3,580 nautical miles and a 5,190 nautical miles range at maximum optional weight, with a 3% fuel factor. Judging by how Boeing is actually flying the aircraft, it is best suited for ranges from 2,000 nautical miles up to around 4,300 nautical miles. Most of Delta's 767-400ER's highest-frequency routes are transatlantic, with the notable exception of the New York-Los Angeles pairing and, to a much lesser extent, the New York-San Francisco route.

#6143. Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

#6142. Amex Blue Cash Preferred Review: A Top Cash Back Card For Everyday Purchases

If you spend a lot at supermarkets and want to earn cash back, the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express is hard to beat. The card offers 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets and on select streaming subscriptions, which can add up fast for families and anyone with a few monthly subscriptions.

In this post, I’ll cover the welcome offer, the bonus categories and how they work, the Disney streaming credit, and how this card compares to other options like the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express and the Citi Strata Premier® Card.

Link: Learn more about the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express

Before I get into the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card review, here’s a quick look at the most important features and fees:

And here are my thoughts on the main pros and cons of the Blue Cash Preferred Card:

When applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome offer, the eligibility, and the fees, are major considerations, given that they can be the first factors that impact interest in a card. So along those lines, let’s take a look at those details for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred is currently offering the following welcome bonus: You may be eligible for as high as $300 cash back after spending $3,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first 6 months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

That’s a solid bonus for a card at this price point, and the six month window gives you plenty of time to hit the spending requirement. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Amex cards tend to be fairly easy to get approved for if you have excellent credit. A few rules to know:

As you can see, this card is marketed as offering a bonus “as high as” a certain amount. The way this works, you can apply for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95. (Rates & Fees). That puts it in line with other mid-range cards. No first year annual fee is a nice perk, as it lets you test the card and see how much value you’re getting before you commit to the ongoing fee.

If you decide the card isn’t working for you after the first year, you can always downgrade to the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday Card.

You can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost, so that their spending can help you rack up rewards.

I wouldn’t recommend using the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card outside the U.S. or for purchases in foreign currencies. The 2.7% foreign transaction fee will eat into your rewards (Rates & Fees). There are plenty of other cards with no foreign transaction fees that are better suited for international spending.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has some excellent bonus categories, especially if you spend a lot at U.S. supermarkets and on streaming. Below is a full breakdown.

This is the headline feature of the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, and it’s the single best cash back rate for U.S. supermarket spending that I’m aware of. You earn 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year in purchases (then 1%). This is the only bonus category with an earning cap.

To put that in perspective, if you spend $500 a month on U.S. supermarket spending, you’d earn $360 per year in cash back from this category alone. That more than covers the $95 annual fee.

Note that supermarkets don’t include superstores, warehouse clubs (like Costco or Sam’s Club), or discount stores. If most of your grocery shopping happens at a traditional supermarket, this card is incredibly rewarding.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred also offers 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming subscriptions. The list of qualifying services is quite long and includes most of the major platforms: Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, ESPN+, HBO Max, Spotify, Apple TV, Apple Music, Amazon Music Unlimited, YouTube Premium, YouTube TV, Peacock, Sling TV, and many more.

If you’re spending $50 to $100 a month across streaming services (which many households are these days), that 6% adds up nicely.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers 3% cash back on transit purchases, including taxis, ridesharing, parking, tolls, trains, and buses. If you commute by public transit or use rideshare services regularly, this is a solid bonus category.

With the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you also earn 3% cash back at eligible U.S. gas stations, with no caps. Note that this doesn’t include gas purchased at superstores, supermarkets, or warehouse clubs that sell fuel.

For purchases that don’t fall into the bonus categories, you earn 1% cash back. This is the one weak spot of the card. At just 1% on non-bonused spending, you’ll want to pair this card with something that earns a better return on everyday purchases (more on that below).

With the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you earn Reward Dollars that can be redeemed as statement credits, and there’s no minimum cash back balance required before you can redeem. It’s simple and straightforward, though it’s worth knowing that you can’t use cash back to pay your minimum payment due.

As is the case for any credit card, it’s also important to consider the benefits and credits offered, if any. The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a reasonable annual fee, so what are the benefits like? Well, they’re potentially pretty solid, and can help justify the annual fee…

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers up to $10 back per month ($120 per year) as a statement credit when you use your enrolled card to purchase a subscription, including a bundle subscription, on DisneyPlus.com, Hulu.com, or Stream.ESPN.com U.S. websites, with no minimum purchase requirement. Subscription is subject to auto-renewal. (Enrollment required)

Another Amex Blue Cash Preferred benefit is access to Amex Presale Tickets® and Amex Reserved Tickets®, which can come in handy if you’re trying to score tickets to an in-demand concert or sporting event.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred also includes an introductory 0% APR offer that can give you some breathing room on purchases and balance transfers.

Enjoy 0% intro APR on purchases and balance transfers for 12 months from the date of account opening. After that, your APR will be a variable APR of 19.74% - 28.74%

This could be helpful if you need to transfer an existing credit card balance and have some time to pay it off before interest kicks in, or if you need some extra time to pay off a big upcoming purchase. Just make sure you pay off your balance in full before the intro period ends, or you’ll be on the hook for interest after all.

One benefit that doesn’t get enough attention is the Amex Offers program. This gives you access to targeted deals with a variety of retailers, just by registering your card and making an eligible purchase.

Different Amex cards get different offers, so having multiple Amex cards in your wallet means more chances to save. Across my Amex cards, this program saves me hundreds of dollars per year.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card has fewer travel protections than more premium Amex cards, but it does come with coverage to protect your rental car when you charge the rental to this card. The coverage applies for eligible damage or theft, and it’s secondary, so it kicks in after your own car insurance. There are some exclusions, and it doesn’t include liability coverage, so check your card benefits guide for the full details.

Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card offers the following benefits when you shop with the card:

These are all helpful benefits that you hopefully won’t have to use (though they do provide some peace of mind). Just remember you need to purchase the relevant items with your card to get this coverage.

Purchase Protection is an embedded benefit of your Card Membership and requires no enrollment. It can help protect Covered Purchases made on your Eligible Card when they’re accidentally damaged, stolen, or lost, for up to 90 days from the Covered Purchase date. The coverage is limited to up to $10,000 per occurrence, up to $50,000 per Card Member account per calendar year. Coverage Limits Apply. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. When an American Express® Card Member charges a Covered Purchase to an Eligible Card, Extended Warranty§ can provide up to one extra year added to the Original Manufacturer’s Warranty. Applies to warranties of five (5) years or less. Coverage is up to the actual amount charged to your Card for the item up to a maximum of $10,000; not to exceed $50,000 per Card Member account per calendar year. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

I tend to lean toward points-earning cards for my own spending, but I totally get why a lot of people prefer cash back. It’s simple, flexible, and you can spend it however you want, including on travel. For that crowd, the Blue Cash Preferred is one of the best options out there.

If you’re someone who is looking to earn cash back and spends a lot at supermarkets, then the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card is an exceptional choice, in my opinion — 6% cash back will add up quickly.

The 6% cash back on streaming, and 3% cash back on transit and gas stations, will add up quickly as well, and up to $120 Disney streaming credit could be worth more than the annual fee.

However, this isn’t the card I would be using for your everyday spending, as you’d only earn 1% cash back in the categories that aren’t eligible for bonuses. So I’d acquire this card specifically with the intent of using it in the categories offering bonuses.

So, let’s take a look at what other cards you should potentially be considering.

If you like the idea of an Amex cash back card but aren’t sure about paying an annual fee, the Blue Cash Everyday Card from American Express (learn more) is the no annual fee alternative where you can earn as high as $200 cash back after spending $2,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first six months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

Here’s how the two Blue Cash cards compare:

In my opinion, the Blue Cash Preferred is well worth the annual fee if you spend a meaningful amount at supermarkets. The jump from 3% to 6% on U.S. supermarkets adds up fast. If you spend $500 a month at supermarkets, that extra 3% earns you $180 more per year, which nearly doubles the annual fee.

The Blue Cash Everyday does have one unique advantage: 3% cash back on U.S. online retail purchases, which the Preferred doesn’t offer. If you do a lot of online shopping and less grocery shopping, the Everyday could actually come out ahead.

The good news is that you can always start with the Blue Cash Preferred and downgrade to the Blue Cash Everyday after the first year if the math doesn’t work out.

If you’re just looking for the simplest cash back credit card, it’s tough to go wrong with the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase, for a total of 2% back on every purchase. That’s a solid return on everyday spending, and you don’t have to keep track of any bonus spending categories.

If you’re deciding between the Blue Cash Preferred and a mid-range card from another issuer, the $95 annual fee Citi Strata Premier Card (learn more) is worth considering. These two cards serve pretty different purposes, but they’re at the same price point:

The Blue Cash Preferred wins on supermarkets and streaming, hands down. If those are your biggest spending categories, the Blue Cash Preferred is the better card.

The Strata Premier is the more well-rounded card overall. It earns 3x points across five major categories (dining, gas, supermarkets, airfare, hotels), has no foreign transaction fees, and its ThankYou points can be transferred to airline and hotel partners for potentially much more than face value. If you travel or eat out a lot, the Strata Premier likely comes out ahead.

One final card worth considering alongside the Blue Cash Preferred Card is the American Express® Gold Card (learn more). It has a significantly higher annual fee, but it’s unbeatable for earning rewards at U.S. supermarkets — you’ll earn transferable Membership Rewards points too, rather than cash back.

The Blue Cash Preferred is the best cash back card for supermarket spending, and it’s not particularly close. If groceries and streaming are a big part of your monthly budget, this card can deliver serious returns, especially with the 6% rate on both categories plus the Disney streaming credit.

The annual fee pays for itself quickly if you’re spending even a moderate amount at supermarkets. Pair it with a card like the Citi Double Cash for your non-bonused spending, and you’ve got a strong cash back setup.

Just keep in mind that the 1% rate on everyday purchases means this card works best as a specialist, not your only card. Use it where it shines, and let a flat-rate card handle the rest.

If you want to learn more about the Blue Cash Preferred Card or want to apply, follow this link.
