The Thanksgiving travel rush is off to a messy start.

The culprit: bad weather and the latest tech outage to hit a major U.S. company.

Delta Air Lines delayed or canceled thousands of flights on Sunday after a problem with a key system that automates weight and balance calculations.

The disruption led to mass delays at its Atlanta mega-hub — the world’s busiest airport — and cascaded to other airports around the country.

By 6:15 p.m. EST Sunday, more than half of all flights had been delayed at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), according to FlightAware. That included hundreds of departing flights — and planes headed to the airport.

Late Sunday afternoon, Delta said it had restored its automated system. But the disruptions continued to climb as the carrier worked to get operations fully back on track.

Delta's residual flight disruptions climbed through the day on Sunday.

Around 70% of the flight disruptions were due to the tech issues, the airline said. The rest were tied to Sunday's weather problems, and air traffic control delays that resulted.

“We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism," Delta said in a statement to TPG.

Travelers had other problems to contend with Sunday, too.

Mother Nature also snarled air traffic at some major hubs.

Low cloud ceilings and poor visibility fueled flight delays and led to dozens of planes getting diverted.

New York’s LaGuardia Airport (LGA) was most heavily affected, with nearly 60% of all departing and arriving flights delayed Sunday, per FlightAware.

42 flights headed to LGA on Sunday were diverted to other airports, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.

Many of those flights landed instead in Philadelphia; Albany, N.Y.; Harrisburg, PA; and Syracuse, N.Y.

These disruptions come a week after one of the most chaotic weekends at airports in recent memory.

More than 18,000 flights were canceled last weekend after an outage on Nov. 13 to critical Federal Aviation Administration technology.

Last week, a brief technical outage at United Airlines also fueled a host of flight delays.

What to do if you’re affected: This week, the TPG team put our heads together to offer some of our top tips for navigating a travel meltdown. Here’s what to know.

If your flight is canceled or significantly delayed, you’re entitled to a refund under U.S. Department of Transportation policy — but only if you choose not to fly.

If you get stranded in Sunday’s travel mess, it pays to know what the reason was for the disruption.

If you get stuck because of Delta’s tech outage, the carrier may be willing to pay for any hotel, meal and ground transportation costs you incur — if it’s a major delay. See details at FlightRights.gov.

The carrier on Sunday acknowledged it was providing those accommodations to passengers "when necessary."

If you get stuck because of bad weather, it's less likely your airline will offer any sort of compensation. But keep your receipts: If you paid for your trip with a credit card that has travel insurance, you might be able to file a claim and seek reimbursement.

Sunday’s travel woes also coincide, of course, with the start of the Thanksgiving travel rush — with airports expected to be very busy with holiday travelers over the next few days.

All eyes are on next Sunday — Nov. 29 — which could be the busiest day of the year to fly.

Last year, the Sunday after Thanksgiving set the record as the most crowded day ever at U.S. airports.

#6042. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot."

In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

Booking a table can be the least exciting part of a night out. However, the platform you use to do it can now earn you rewards worth anything from a few cents to a delicious discount on your bill.

OpenTable, DoorDash, Seated and now Resy all reward you for dining out, though each takes a different approach. OpenTable awards its own points, DoorDash issues credits for future orders, Seated offers rewards that can be redeemed for gift cards and Resy awards American Express Membership Rewards points.

As with your favorite coffee chain's loyalty program or a food delivery app subscription, the best option depends on where, how often and how much you eat out. Whichever you choose, you'll generally still earn rewards on eligible restaurant purchases when paying with a dining credit card, making your meal even sweeter.

In this guide, we compare what each program earns, what those rewards are worth and the fine print to watch so you can decide which one deserves a seat at your table.

*Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations.

Related: This overlooked dining program is one of the most generous and gets you $25 off your very first meal

OpenTable Regulars is free to join, and you'll earn 100 dining points for each reservation you book directly on OpenTable while signed in to your account and then complete. Reservations made through restaurant websites or third-party booking partners generally don't qualify. Points are posted only after you've dined, so canceled reservations and no-shows earn nothing.

Some restaurants in the program also offer bonus-point reservations worth 500, 750 or even 1,000 points at certain times. To find them, turn on the "bonus points filter" under special features in the OpenTable app.

Once you have at least 1,000 points, you can redeem them in the app's "Rewards" section at the following rates for U.S. members:

As for the redemption rate you'll get for each, they're:

That means a standard 100-point reservation is only worth 80 cents toward a future meal, and you'll need 20 of them to earn a $16 dining credit, which isn't very rewarding.

Dining credits work at participating OpenTable restaurants (look for the "Dining Credit Accepted" filter). After you redeem your points, you can add the credit to a reservation, which provides a digital Mastercard you can use toward eligible bills. Experience credits work similarly but only apply to certain prepaid experiences, such as prix-fixe menus and cocktail classes. Dining credits expire 12 months after you redeem them.

If you complete six reservations on OpenTable within 12 months, you'll then unlock Gold status for a year. Gold members get priority notifications when tables open up, a three-month complimentary Uber One trial for eligible new or returning members who do not have an active subscription and access to "Gold Tables," which promises harder-to-book tables at more than 500 participating restaurants in over 50 U.S. cities.

OpenTable also partners with Chase, Uber and Visa. Uber One members can book Uber One Exclusive Tables, eligible Visa cardholders can access tables and special events through the Visa Dining Collection and select Chase cardholders get exclusive tables and statement credits (more on that below).

Make sure you're actually turning up for your bookings, though. OpenTable will close your Regulars account and cancel all your points if you record four no-shows within 12 months. Your points also expire after 12 months of inactivity or after 3 years from the date you earn them, whichever comes first.

Related: Earn even more rewards when dining out with OpenTable

DoorDash is best known for delivery, but reservations are now available in select cities across the U.S., Australia and Canada. Its current market page lists 17 U.S. cities, plus Melbourne and Sydney in Australia and Toronto and Vancouver in Canada.

Rather than earn points, you earn promotional DoorDash credits when you book and complete an eligible reservation in the DoorDash app or on its website. The amount is shown before you book and now varies by restaurant, reservation time and membership status. Current U.S. listings commonly advertise $5 in credits, while some times display $10 or $12. Not every reservation earns a credit.

Credits are posted after you've paid for your meal and can be used toward eligible future DoorDash delivery or pickup orders. They typically can't be used to pay for taxes, fees or tips, expire six months after they're issued unless the offer says otherwise, have no cash value and can't be used to buy gift cards or alcohol.

Since the reward is a fixed amount, you don't earn more rewards for a higher food bill. A $5 credit is a 5% return on a $100 dinner but about 1.7% on a $300 tasting menu. A $10 credit would deliver returns of 10% and about 3.3%, respectively. That makes DoorDash Reservations especially appealing for smaller restaurant bills if you already use DoorDash.

DashPass members can earn more on eligible reservations, plus access exclusive prime-time tables and discounts on Lyft Black rides. However, the elevated reservation reward is no longer a simple fixed $2 boost across every listing, so check the offer shown before booking rather than assuming your membership guarantees a particular amount.

Check the restaurant's cancellation policy when you book. Late cancellations and no-shows may incur fees set by the restaurant, and DoorDash says excessive no-shows can result in suspension of your access to reservations.

Outside its reservation cities, DoorDash's "Going Out" tab also lists in-store offers at certain restaurants, with DashPass members earning extra rewards for repeat visits in some locations.

Related: Your complete guide to Chase and DoorDash

What is unique about this program is that you don't need to book through Seated: You link an eligible credit or debit card, then tap to activate the restaurants where you want to earn a higher reward rate before paying with your linked card. Eligible rewards then post automatically, with no receipts to upload.

Activations last until the end of the calendar month, and you can activate up to 25 restaurants per month (plus any monthly specials). Seated's app also advertises 5% back at participating restaurants, even without an activation, provided you open the app at least once every 30 days. Higher reward rates generally require activation, so it's worth activating your favorites at the start of each month and checking the offer terms in the app.

Rewards vary by restaurant but can be up to a generous 35% back, with the rate shown on each restaurant's page before you choose to activate it. Rewards are calculated on your eligible food-and-beverage total before tax and tip, so a restaurant offering 10% back would earn you $10 in Seated rewards on a $100 meal. Since each diner earns on the share they pay with their own linked card, splitting the bill doesn't cost anyone their individual rewards.

Seated partners with more than 2,500 restaurants in certain U.S. markets. Availability varies by city and neighborhood, so check the app for participating locations and current rewards before dining, rather than relying on a fixed city list.

You can then redeem Seated rewards for gift cards in the app's store tab, with available brands to choose from including Airbnb, Amazon, Dunkin', Nordstrom, Sephora, Starbucks, Target and Uber. Because rewards can then be converted to eligible gift cards at face value, TPG values them at $1 per $1 redeemed, provided you choose a brand you'd spend with anyway and meet any minimum redemption requirement.

The catch is that Seated rewards may expire after more than 30 days without qualifying account activity, so check the app's activity and expiration rules rather than assuming opening it alone preserves your balance. Seated also says its rewards can't be combined with other restaurant promotions, third-party deals (such as those available through Groupon) or discount offers.

If you're a new member, keep an eye out for a first-meal bonus offer of up to $10 through an eligible referral link or promotional offer, though this is not guaranteed for every member.

Related: Rove adds dining and in-store rewards in major platform expansion

Resy Rewards takes a different approach than the other three programs. It does not issue a stand-alone Resy currency. Instead, eligible U.S. American Express cardmembers earn 4 additional Membership Rewards points per dollar spent at participating restaurants, on top of the points their enrolled card already earns.

To participate, you must first enroll an eligible U.S. Amex card that earns Membership Rewards points in the Rewards tab of the Resy iOS app.

You must then book a participating restaurant through the Rewards tab, complete the meal and pay with the enrolled card. Merely dining at a participating restaurant or booking it through another part of Resy will not trigger the 4 bonus points per dollar. At launch, the program is only available through the Resy iOS app, meaning Android users cannot currently use it.

The initial New York City list includes restaurants like Carne Mare, Le Crocodile, Hearth, Kiko, Opto and Le Pavillon. American Express plans to expand Resy Rewards to additional U.S. cities and select Tock venues in 2027.

On a $100 eligible restaurant purchase, Resy Rewards would provide 400 bonus Membership Rewards points. Based on our valuation of 2 cents per Membership Rewards point, that is an estimated $8 in value (or an 8% return) before accounting for the card's standard earning rate.

Related: Don't overlook Resy: How to maximize dining experiences and save money with this Amex benefit

Because OpenTable and DoorDash reward reservations with a fixed amount while Seated pays a percentage of your bill and Resy pays a fixed number of points per dollar spent, the best option depends on how much you spend. Here's a comparison for $100 in food-and-drink purchases (before tax and tip), assuming the advertised offers apply and you can use the full value of the DoorDash credits on a later order:

If you spend $200 on a meal rather than $100, the OpenTable and DoorDash rewards stay the same, while the Seated rewards as a percentage of spending will quickly increase. Resy would also double to 800 bonus points, worth an estimated $16 with TPG's valuation of Amex points.

Seated can be the most rewarding option for larger restaurant bills, especially at restaurants that offer higher reward rates. However, its value depends on the percentage offered. DoorDash's fixed credits may still provide you with a better return on smaller bills or at restaurants that offer lower Seated rewards. Resy provides a consistent 8% estimated return from its bonus points — but only at its small number of participating restaurants at launch.

Related: The dining statement credits that save me over $1,000 every year

Certain restaurant purchases can also earn credit card rewards in addition to the benefits provided by these platforms. Combining these apps with a card that earns bonus points at restaurants can be an easy way to double-dip and earn more rewards. Some of the best options currently available include:

But it gets even better. Savvy diners keen on maximizing their rewards may be able to triple-dip by booking an eligible Sapphire Reserve Exclusive Tables restaurant through OpenTable and paying with their Sapphire Reserve card. Doing so will allow you to earn OpenTable Regulars points plus 3 Chase Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent on the eligible dining purchase, even if you later receive a statement credit. Qualifying purchases at participating restaurants can also trigger the separate Sapphire Reserve dining credit, worth up to $150 per half-year.

Related: How to double-, triple- or even quadruple-dip on dining rewards

Resy Rewards offers a strong, straightforward points return at participating restaurants. However, the program is launching at only a handful of New York City restaurants and is available through the Resy iOS app, so most diners will not be able to use it regularly yet.

Seated has the highest potential return for larger dining bills. A restaurant offering 15% back would earn you $30 in rewards redeemable for gift cards on a $200 dinner, while a 35% offer would earn $70. Know, though, that higher rates generally require monthly activation, and you'll need to keep your rewards account active.

DoorDash Reservations can still be the best option for smaller meals when the booking carries a strong credit. A $10 or $12 reward can beat percentage-based programs on a modest check. The catch is that rewards now vary by reservation, availability is limited to select cities and the credits are less useful if you rarely order through DoorDash.

OpenTable Regulars is the least rewarding of the four for most standard reservations, with a 100-point booking worth just 80 cents at the best U.S. redemption rate. Still, it is the most broadly available of the four in the markets where its Dining Points program operates and offers useful extras, including bonus-point tables, Gold Tables and a three-month Uber One trial for eligible Gold members. Select Chase cardholders can also receive statement credits at eligible restaurants.

There's no single best dining rewards platform for everyone, as the right choice depends on where you live, how much you spend and how often you dine out.

Resy offers a compelling points return at participating venues, but its limited launch footprint and lack of an Android app make it more of a promising option than an everyday solution right now.

Seated can deliver the biggest reward on an expensive meal, while DoorDash can be particularly rewarding on a smaller bill when the booking offers a decent credit.

As for OpenTable, it remains the most broadly available of the four in the markets where its Dining Points program operates. Its nationwide coverage, Gold perks and Chase partnership make it worth considering, especially when you travel.

Since all four cost nothing to join, you may as well sign up for them all so you are ready the next time you want to book a meal. Just remember to show up for reservations or cancel within the restaurant's deadline, as no-shows can cost you points, credits or even access.

That's some food for thought before your next night out.

#6037. The Complex Reputation of James Burnham

The political theorist was known for his detachment — both in his political views and in his daily life.

James Burnham appears on an episode of Firing Line in 1978.

The British first edition of The Managerial Revolution that I picked up in a Charing Cross Road shop a quarter century ago tells us much about the work itself. I’ve read it four times, conscripted it as an airplane companion, and brought it to the beach. Yet its binding remains strong, its cover quite flexible, and its pages yellowing but intact. We no longer much refer to let alone read such 1941 bestsellers as Clifton Fadiman’s Reading I’ve Liked or Margaret Leech’s Reveille in Washington. But James Burnham, much like my strong and solid copy of his most famous book, endures.

Burnham, who entered the world 121 years ago Sunday and left it nearly 40 years ago, very much remains part of the Great Conversation. The Managerial Revolution, anticipating as it did the ascension of technocrats, specialists, and the bureaucratic elite as a sort of ruling class, surely helped in that regard. Burnham remains read, despite no Burnhamite clique in academia or organized faction among movement conservatives dedicated to advancing his ideas. Kirkians, Straussians, and Randians exist. Why no James Burnham Preservation Society with an accompanying secret handshake?

Daniel J. Flynn, the author of The Man Who Invented Conservatism: The Unlikely Life of Frank S. Meyer, is an American Spectator senior editor, visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution, and YouTuber @RightWingWilderness.

#6034. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

As much as I love the holiday season, it's my least favorite time to travel. Flights and accommodations are expensive, airports are at their busiest and winter storms can upend even the best-laid plans.

A credit card can't help your family pack lighter or ensure your flight departs on time. But the right benefits can lessen the sting from some of travel's most predictable pain points.

Here are the cards that can make the biggest difference during a hectic holiday trip, organized by the problem they solve.

Few travel fees are more annoying than paying extra to bring your socks with you — especially now that roundtrip bag fees can feel higher than the cost of the clothes inside.

For a family checking multiple bags, this may be the most immediately valuable benefit on this list. A card with a relatively modest annual fee can pay for itself during holiday travel alone.

Many airline credit cards offer a free checked bag, so start with the airline you fly most.

Higher-fee airline cards often match or exceed the checked-bag benefits shown here.

Many of the same airline cards that waive bag fees also provide priority boarding benefits. On a packed holiday flight, I'll gladly get in line early if it keeps my carry-on out of the gate-check pile.

The $895 annual fee (see rates and fees) offers another way to lower the cost of bags or boarding. Its up to $200 annual airline incidental credit can reimburse eligible expenses such as checked bag and seat selection fees with one selected qualifying airline (enrollment required). This is a useful way for existing cardmembers to absorb a holiday expense.

The (see rates and fees) offers a broader alternative: Its $300 annual travel credit applies automatically to eligible travel purchases, including checked bag fees.

Related: Which airline credit cards offer the best priority boarding perks?

Ever spend more time in airport security than you do on the flight itself? TSA PreCheck, Global Entry and Clear+ earn their keep throughout November and December.

PreCheck provides expedited screening at eligible U.S. airports; Global Entry includes PreCheck and adds expedited processing when returning to the U.S. from abroad; and Clear+ uses biometric identity verification to speed up the document-check step of security (so some travelers use it alongside PreCheck).

And for travelers who frequently cross between the U.S. and Canada, Nexus can speed up passport control.

You don't necessarily need a premium card to get these application fees reimbursed. Options include:

I like this benefit because it works regardless of which airline you're flying and gives you something that's often in limited supply: time. Just apply well before your trip because Trusted Traveler applications take some time to process. You can't open a card on Monday and expect to breeze through security on Friday.

The information for the U.S. Bank Altitude Connect has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

A lounge won't make a delayed flight leave sooner, but a power outlet, snacks and a drink make the wait easier.

These lounge cards offer different benefits:

* Up to 10 visits per eligible Platinum Card, per year to the Delta Sky Club or to Grab and Go when traveling on a same-day Delta-operated flight

I've had all of these over the years, although lately my favorite card for lounge access is the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite. The card's Priority Pass membership still provides credits at participating airport restaurants, which can be helpful when traditional lounges are full or there's nowhere left to sit.

There's a broader lesson there, too: don't choose a card based solely on how many lounges its network advertises. Check whether your airports have participating locations, whether there are restrictions on when you can visit and if it costs extra to bring your travel companions.

The information for the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: Is the Amex Platinum worth the annual fee?

Some premium-card credits seem easy to overlook until you arrive at midnight with no energy to navigate public transportation and ride-hailing fares are surging.

Food-delivery credits are also surprisingly useful at the hotel. I recently had Uber Eats delivered to my hotel because taking a cranky kid to dinner wasn't my idea of a good time.

For Uber users, both the and stand out. The Gold offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually (distributed as up to $10 each month), while the Platinum offers up to $200 in Uber Cash annually (up to $15 each month, plus an additional $20 in December) for U.S. Uber rides and Uber Eats orders.

Uber Cash will only be deposited into one Uber account when you add the Amex Gold or Amex Platinum as a payment method and redeem with any Amex card.

Platinum cardmembers can also receive up to a $120 statement credit for an auto-renewing Uber One membership, Uber's paid membership program for ride and delivery savings (enrollment required).

The counters with up to $420 in DoorDash credits (a monthly $15 promo for any eligible order plus two $10 nonrestaurant promos, through Dec. 31, 2029).

Its complimentary DashPass membership (activate by Dec. 31, 2029) also unlocks Lyft Go at no additional cost, allowing you to earn Lyft credits on eligible rides. Separately, Sapphire Reserve cardholders receive up to $10 in monthly Lyft ride credits through Sep. 30, 2027. (You'll need to link your DoorDash and Lyft accounts and claim Lyft Go.)

These credits alone are not reasons to pay hundreds of dollars in annual fees. But they can be genuinely useful when you're otherwise staring down an expensive ride or going to bed hungry.

Hotel timing benefits are especially useful when checkout is at 11 a.m., your flight leaves after dinner and no one wants to tote an overstuffed diaper bag around for six hours while your toddler desperately needs a nap.

There are two ways a credit card can help: through a premium hotel-booking program or automatic hotel elite status.

Those looking for boutique hotel experiences can access The Edit by Chase Travel℠ with their . These bookings provide benefits like daily breakfast for two people and a $100 property credit. When available, early check-in, late checkout and room upgrades are also offered. Cardholders receive up to $500 annually in statement credits for eligible prepaid The Edit bookings (of at least two nights; split into two credits of up to $250 each).

Similarly, cardmembers can receive up to $300 in statement credits biannually (up to $600 per calendar year) on eligible prepaid bookings through Fine Hotels + Resorts, The Hotel Collection and Airbnb Luxe through American Express Travel®.

FHR bookings include guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout, daily breakfast for two and property or experience credits. Room upgrades and early check-in are also offered (subject to availability).

(THC and Airbnb Luxe bookings require a minimum stay of two consecutive nights. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, FHR bookings will also require at least two nights to qualify for the lodging statement credit.)

These programs can be valuable when a nicer property is already part of the plan or you have annual hotel credits to use. Just don't let a possible upgrade or a few extra hours rationalize a room that costs twice as much as the hotel across the street.

Many hotel credit cards offer complimentary elite status. For example, the $95-per-year (see rates and fees) includes Discoverist status, which comes with 2 p.m. late checkout (when available).

Top-tier Globalist status extends that to a 4 p.m. checkout. The Hyatt card can help you work toward it with five qualifying-night credits each year plus two additional credits for every $5,000 spent.

Related: World of Hyatt Credit Card review: My favorite mid-tier hotel card

Hotel breakfast is one of those expenses that seems harmless until you're buying it for several people for several mornings.

These cards can help lower breakfast costs:

cardmembers can enroll in Hilton Gold status and receive breakfast or food-and-beverage benefits rather than having to apply for a Hilton card separately.

Rental car status is rarely about an upgrade from a sedan to an SUV, especially during a sold-out holiday week. The most valuable benefit is simply getting into a car and leaving the airport while everyone else is still waiting at the counter.

Capital One Venture X cardholders can enroll in Hertz President's Circle status**, which offers benefits including skip-the-line privileges, a wider vehicle selection, potential upgrades and a free additional driver. Meanwhile, the $95 Venture Rewards offers lower-tier Hertz Five Star** status.

cardholders receive Avis Preferred Plus and National Executive status, and cardmembers can enroll in complimentary elite status with Avis, Hertz and National.

In every case, the key is to enroll. Sign up and confirm your status appears in your account before you leave home.

**Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (i.e., at hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program, and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

Related: How to stack Venture X earning and Hertz elite benefits

These perks are only useful if they are ready when you need them. Before your trip:

Related: 4 things you really need to do now in advance of holiday travel

For holiday travel, the best card isn't necessarily the one with the longest list of premium benefits; it's the one that solves the problem most likely to cost you money or patience. A family checking several bags may save more with a $95 airline card than an $895 premium card, while someone planning a dream trip may want every perk they can get.

Opening an expensive card solely to make one trip less miserable isn't the play here. But if you are already paying a premium annual fee, this is the time to use the benefits you've paid for all year.

#6032. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#6031. The American Genius of Madden

David O. Russell pays tribute to football, folklore, and eccentricity.

Chuck ZlotnickAmazon Content Services LLC

Hang on at the start of David O. Russell’s Madden, as its story of the Oakland Raiders football coach John Madden shifts between semidocumentary and biopic. Russell’s uneven, sketchy narrative steadily turns into a probing human comedy. It’s also a slyly monumental tale of American genius found in an Everyman’s commonplace ambition.

The key to the film’s geniality and surprise is Nicolas Cage’s astounding portrayal of Madden, a former college athlete who blew out his knee but kept his feeling for football. Cage enters the mindset of a sports fanatic who is also an artist, devising plays and strategies that, considering his size and vision, earn him the nickname “Buddha.” But this is not one of those freak-outs that Cage is known for; he seems to transform himself into John Candy — broad-beamed with a tuft of blond hair and a convincing smile. Cage commits to this genial eccentric who, despite his unreachable idiosyncrasy, is harmless, lovable yet tough — an authentic, original American.

Madden became coach for the Raiders, a team known to play with sheer guts and dedication — qualities the burly Buddha shared with team owner Al Davis (Christian Bale), his wiry, sharklike best friend. This thick-and-thin Laurel-and-Hardy pair sustain an unlikely partnership. It’s one of the most remarkable depictions of brotherhood in movies — a friendship that persists over temperamental tensions, even after Madden leaves the team and pursues media entrepreneurship to sustain his love of the sport. Madden the broadcaster converts his playbook ingenuity and follows his father’s advice: “Get away with doing what you love for as long as you possibly can.”

Russell redeems himself with the oddest-yet-normal collection of American eccentrics. Acting on the edge of parody, Cage and Bale, with their uncanny sincerity, reward Russell’s interest in quirkiness. (Madden hears Davis’s voice in his head.) The fascinating scoundrels of Russell’s terrific American Hustle were preoccupied with manipulating one another. Here, friendship, comradeship, teamwork, and family complications are genuinely recognizable. Scenes that emulate a documentary approach — Madden’s wife Virginia (gung ho comedienne Kathryn Hahn) rivals Jennifer Lawrence’s volatility when speaking directly to the camera — satirize realism to fulfill the non-cynical view of national character that Russell fumbled in the bohemian sojourn of Amsterdam. No wonder De Niro is left out of this particular silver-lined playbook.

The patchwork of styles in Madden suggests that Russell investigates American eccentricity as he goes along, finding his way back to the coast-to-coast realness that made his Flirting with Disaster so exhilarating (as in Madden’s surreal, unapologetic pitch for the unique holiday dish the Turducken). Russell adopts Madden’s football-analysis style, such as on-screen telestrator vectors, to humorously examine Madden’s own career shifts and twists of personality (Madden instructing his players, or meeting colleagues Pat Summerall, Howard Cosell, and Bob Costas).

A dull-witted filmmaker, say James Cameron, would choose an “immersive” style for a movie concerned with the gestalt of football. But Russell’s film is also about the phenomenon of a sport that becomes a vanguard of technology and culture. Madden is pursued by Trip Hawkins (John Mulaney), founder of video game company EA (Electronic Arts), who wants to translate Madden’s football theories for a new generation of at-home fans and gamers. Hawkins’s proposal is scored to Beethoven’s Ninth — another example of Russell’s wit, matching the film’s eclectic score from Barry White and Talking Heads to N.W.A. (“You don’t want to know what that means,” Davis says to Madden.)

Through Madden and Hawkins’s acumen, Russell treats the discovery of a new world as an aftereffect of folk intelligence and ingenuity. Genius is kidded when Hawkins’s team of four-eyed computer nerds demonstrate jock potential after applying Madden’s plays to their algorithms. It’s a sweet way of conveying the phenomenon that would turn EA’s Madden NFL video game franchise into a $4 billion enterprise (some estimates raise that into double digits), with annual compensation going to the Madden family estate.

More important, Russell (who co-wrote the script with Cambron Clark) sees Madden as a visionary who proudly summarizes TV sportscasting as “They state the obvious, which is f***ing boring.” My only complaint is that Robert Richardson’s photography tends toward frowzy (perhaps deliberately aping TV docs), not as splendid as Oliver Stone’s Any Given Sunday — the greatest football movie ever made.

Madden itself shares biopic sensibility with John Ford’s The Wings of Eagles, respectfully eschewing its subject’s mortality for an optimistic appreciation of a man’s potential. It is unique to American character and the experience of competition and dreams of the NFL Hall of Fame that Madden shared with Al Davis. Russell’s tribute comes complete with a motto: “You make people feel good and alive and good to be American, and I’m not standing in the way of that.” Thus Russell proves his own resilience and the achievement of a new folkloric genre struggling to emerge.

Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

#6029. Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”

“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”

During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”

Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”

#6028. On Personalized Pricing, the FTC Got Ahead of the Evidence

The agency pulled a market failure out of thin air and tasked itself with solving it.

Delta Airlines passenger jets at LaGuardia Airport in Queens, N.Y., in 2022.

Americans should expect their federal agencies to be staffed by experts who gather evidence meticulously before proposing regulations disinterestedly. But that’s not what the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has done when it comes to personalized pricing.

Last month, the FTC ordered nine major companies — Delta Air Lines, Uber, and Instacart among them — “to provide detailed information that will allow the agency to study the use of personal data to set prices and compensation.” The agency, however, seems to have reached its conclusions already, given the contents of both its order and an enforcement policy proposed in August, which appears partial against personalized pricing and the businesses that employ it.

Vladlena Klymova is a policy analyst at the Taxpayers Protection Alliance.

On “On Personalized Pricing, the FTC Got Ahead of the Evidence”

#6026. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

#6025. An Overhyped Trilateral Summit

U.S. President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China’s President Xi Jinping stands beside at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, November 18, 2026.

Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin have now concluded their first-ever trilateral meeting. Each leader has pronounced himself satisfied with their discussion. But if their concluding statement is an accurate reflection of what was said in the closed session, little of any real consequence — with one possible exception — was agreed to, which was only to be expected. Much has been made by some of the symbolism of the meeting. Did it signal that a disreputable carve-up, even a new Yalta, was underway? If that was the plan, the result, appropriately and mercifully, looks like a package with more than a touch of Temu about it.

That is not to deny that some of the optics involved were grating. Trump’s earlier, overly enthusiastic greeting of his “friend” Putin — the aggressor, after all, in a genocidal war — was not only nauseating but also careless. It sent a disturbing signal to the rest of NATO, an organization that still plays a critical role in maintaining American security as well as peace, however uneasy, in Europe west of Ukraine. It is to be hoped that Trump’s delight at the sight of his supposed pal was, to use a word often applied to this president’s approach to diplomacy, transactional, a display of a dealmaker’s schmooze and nothing more.

The fact that Putin was in the room has attracted criticism for its symbolic “confirmation” of Russia as one of, to borrow a term from the real Yalta, the “big three.” Not so much: Putin’s presence merely reflected geopolitical reality, something that, however unpleasant, cannot be wished away. Russia is economically enfeebled and embroiled in a brutally and humiliatingly debilitating war, but it remains a vast, resource-rich country that, militarily anyway, counts as a superpower and one that, as Ukrainians can testify, is still capable of wreaking immense destruction. The more interesting symbolism was detectable in the various gestures through which Xi Jinping emphasized during Putin’s visit that Russia is China’s junior partner. That, too, is today’s reality.

As alluded to above, the joint statement issued after the meeting was, as should have been expected, thin gruel. There was talk of reforming the U.N. “so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfil its fundamental mission of maintaining international peace and security.” If that implies reining in Turtle Bay’s efforts to extend supranational (and thus post-democratic) governance, that’s no bad thing, but in practice little will probably change.

In a similar vein, the trio, whose countries have not submitted to the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, implicitly criticized the attempted extension of its reach. They stressed the need for “respect for immunities of State officials,” a subject doubtless close to Putin’s heart. There is no need to grumble too much about this. The ICC is highly politicized, and, while it does not constitute much of a deterrent, it may even provide a perverse incentive to wrongdoers to hang onto power. Putin deserves to face judgment, but a better place for that would be Kyiv, not The Hague.

And all three declared that they planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.” If that reflected some post-midterms unease on Trump’s part, that, as an admission of weakness, would have been a message better not sent. It would also be a mistake, despite recent waivers, for the U.S. to abandon its general application of sanctions on Iranian and Russian oil (the Europeans, incidentally, could do a better job of enforcing theirs). No pressure should be put on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure other than as part of a general “energy cease-fire” such as that floated earlier this year, which Ukraine was willing to accept.

No details have been released so far of what was said in the meeting about Ukraine. However, Putin has been reiterating his hard line, supplemented by an absurd and aggressive proposal to rewrite Europe’s security architecture. Hopefully, Trump was not misled by any bonhomie in Shenzhen, although some accounts of his later call with European leaders were not entirely encouraging in that respect.

From left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump participate in a trilateral meeting during the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, November 19, 2026.

To return to reality: China has no interest in helping end the war in Ukraine, and Russia’s ambitions in Europe are such that the eventual consequences of undermining Kyiv’s ability to resist won’t stop at Ukraine’s borders. Speaking of which, we hope that Trump warned Xi and Putin that the growing intensity of “gray zone” activity, from drones in Leipzig Airport to cyberattacks on both sides of the Atlantic, risks triggering retaliation that could easily spiral into something extremely dangerous.

Any claims that the Shenzhen meeting has delivered the death blow to the post-1945 order would be overblown, akin to complaining about the murder of a corpse. The postwar settlement has been in flux for decades — Nixon, after all, went to China — a process that has accelerated, along with dramatic shifts in relative global economic and political power, since the Soviet collapse. But although the landscape has changed, Trump should pay more attention to America’s successful management of the (first) Cold War. Alliances matter, deterrence works, strength is rewarded, and aggression by, or sponsored by, hostile powers and their proxies should be contained and, where possible, reversed.

The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

#6024. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

A dozen cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties raised or updated lodging taxes in recent elections as cities prepare for a surge in visitors during the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

Five months after Los Angeles voters rejected an increase to the city’s lodging tax, the surrounding suburbs hiked their own.

Preliminary results show 12 cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties approving changes to lodging taxes on November 3, according to the California Local Government Finance Almanac. Ten created or raised rates, with two cities pushing their hotel rates above Los Angeles’ 14% tax. Two expanded their current tax to cover more types of stays.

The changes come as Los Angeles and the surrounding area prepare for a surge in visitation for the 2028 Olympics, which are expected to draw in roughly 2 million visitors to the greater Los Angeles area, and as local lawmakers work to address widening budget gaps. Skift previously reported that lodging taxes can be an easy sell because the people paying them aren’t usually locals who vote.

Five months after Los Angeles voters rejected Measure TT, which would have raised the city's 14% lodging tax to 16%, 12 cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties approved lodging tax changes on November 3, according to preliminary results from the California Local Government Finance Almanac. Ten cities created or raised rates, and two expanded coverage to more types of stays. Hawthorne, which borders Inglewood and its Olympic venues, jumped from 12% to 17% and expects as much as $3.1 million in annual revenue. Lynwood approved its first hotel tax at 12%, and Orange and Placentia each went from 10% to 14%. The revenue goes to general funds rather than tourism-specific uses, and the measures come as the region prepares for roughly 2 million visitors for the 2028 Olympics and as local lawmakers work to address widening budget gaps. Short-term rentals lost some of their tax edge: Alhambra extended its 12% occupancy tax to vacation rentals, Monterey Park will tax short-term rental guests at 16% against 14% for hotels, and Santa Monica's council can now apply the lodging tax to corporate stays over 30 days during "major event periods." Statewide, 29 of 34 lodging tax measures were passing, the second largest wave in a decade. Outside California, results were mixed — Tulsa nearly doubled its rate to 9.9% with hotel association backing and tourism earmarks, while voters in Oklahoma, Oregon, Florida, and Mississippi rejected measures.
